librarianNotes.text: The archive opened its doors this month, and what a founding it was: sixteen spells bound in a single July week. Midway through, we made a choice that will shape every shelf to come — this is a library of personal magic now, and the empire-builders were kindly shown the door. Life admin runs the busiest shelf at five tomes, and I notice the strongest spells share one trick: they remember things about their caster. Best find of the month: the fitness plan that reads your sleep and quietly reschedules your training — magic that meets you where you actually are. — the librarian

usecases.title: "Software for an audience of one" — hyper-personal micro-apps
usecases.summary: People vibe-code apps no company would ever ship because the market is exactly one household: a 'Tinder for dinner' decision app for a family with ADHD, a shopping list sorted by their specific grocery store's aisle order, a treadmill remote wired to Google Maps Street View.
usecases.example: A WHOOP-band tracker that correlates heart-rate spikes with calendar events to rank coworkers by how much stress they cause.

recipe.how: Pick one household annoyance and describe the app you wish existed in a short brief: who uses it, the one screen it needs, what data it holds. Let Claude Code scaffold it as a static web app, then iterate by actually using it for a week and telling Claude what annoyed you.

sources.title: XDA Developers — 6 things worth stealing

usecases.title: Life admin & computer janitor work
usecases.summary: Pointing Claude Code at your home directory to rename tax invoices to a consistent format, find duplicate files, organize downloads, batch-convert media, and diagnose a slow Mac. It runs locally with file access, so it handles tedious work chat-based AI can't touch.
usecases.example: Auto-renaming invoices to 'YYYY-MM-DD Vendor - Invoice - Product.pdf' across a messy folder.

recipe.how: Run claude in the messy directory and ask it to inventory the chaos first — a report, no changes. Then approve a naming/folder scheme and let it execute, moving anything questionable to a staging folder instead of deleting.

sources.title: MakeUseOf — non-coding uses
Lenny's Newsletter — everyone should use Claude Code

usecases.title: Creative media projects: audiobooks, games, and extending Claude itself
usecases.summary: Standout: Alexandria, an open-source tool that turns any e-book into a fully voiced multi-cast audiobook — an LLM annotates speakers and delivery directions, local TTS performs it, voice cloning included. Also popular: retro 2D games and custom MCP servers.
usecases.example: Alexandria converts epub/txt/md into multi-voice audiobooks entirely locally, exporting MP3/M4B.

recipe.how: Start from an existing open-source project (like Alexandria) or ask Claude Code to scaffold the pipeline: parse the source material, add an LLM annotation pass for structure, then render with a local engine (TTS, canvas, game loop). Keep it all local.
tools: a local TTS engine or HTML canvas

sources.title: XDA Developers — 6 things worth stealing
KDnuggets — 5 fun projects

usecases.title: TDD with Claude Code: the red-green-refactor loop
usecases.summary: Developers force Claude Code into strict test-driven development: write a failing test (red), let Claude write the minimum code to pass (green), then refactor with the tests as a safety net. It fixes the classic AI failure mode of writing tests that merely mirror the implementation, and practitioners call it one of the few workflows where the model outperforms most humans.
usecases.example: Refactoring a 600-line component in under ten minutes while keeping every test green, with characterization tests written first as the safety net.

recipe.how: Add a TDD rule to CLAUDE.md (or a hook) that forbids implementation before a failing test exists. Then work the loop: describe the behavior, have Claude write the failing test, approve it, and only then let it implement until green.

sources.title: StackNotice — Claude Code TDD workflow
AY Automate — 8 production workflows

usecases.title: A second brain: Claude Code as librarian of your Obsidian vault
usecases.summary: An Obsidian vault is just a folder of markdown, so people run Claude Code inside it as a self-organizing knowledge base: drop in any raw source and Claude reads, tags, links, and files it into a connected graph you own. Then you query it in plain language and it pulls mental models from across every discipline you've ever saved.
usecases.example: The open-source claude-obsidian project, based on Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern, auto-files anything you drop in as linked plain-markdown notes.

recipe.how: Open Claude Code inside your Obsidian vault (it's just a folder) and write a short CLAUDE.md describing your structure and note conventions. Feed it raw material — articles, transcripts, ideas — and ask it to file, tag, and cross-link; query the vault in plain language whenever you need to think.

sources.title: WhyTryAI — second brain with Claude Code & Obsidian
GitHub — claude-obsidian

usecases.title: Ditch the budgeting app: bank statements to a private finance dashboard
usecases.summary: People drop bank statement exports into a folder and have Claude Code categorize transactions, compute savings rates, and build an interactive HTML spending dashboard — processed locally, nothing uploaded. Some log expenses to it in natural language from their phone.
usecases.example: One writer ditched their budgeting app for Claude plus a spreadsheet and says their spending 'finally stopped spiraling.'

recipe.how: Export a few months of bank statements (CSV or PDF) into a folder and ask Claude Code to categorize transactions and generate an HTML dashboard with monthly trends and a savings rate. Re-run monthly with new statements; refine the categories as it learns your patterns.

sources.title: XDA — I ditched my budgeting app for Claude
Claude Code Playbooks — finance manager

usecases.title: The Morning Briefing
usecases.summary: Claude Code pulls your calendar, inbox, meeting notes, and open commitments into a single prioritized daily briefing you can scan in two minutes. People wire it to a session-start hook so it runs automatically when they open Claude in the morning.
usecases.example: A start hook that greets you with today's meetings, the three emails that matter, and what you promised people yesterday.

recipe.how: Connect Gmail and Google Calendar (built-in connectors or MCP), write a briefing prompt that ranks what needs attention, and wire it to a Claude Code session-start hook so it runs unprompted each morning.

sources.title: Harper Reed — Claude Code does my email
Alex Honchar — a personal AI chief of staff

usecases.title: Inbox Triage, Draft-Never-Send
usecases.summary: Claude classifies recent email, learns your voice from past threads, and writes replies saved as drafts in the right thread — never sent without review. The safety rail is what makes it usable.
usecases.example: Waking up to a triaged inbox where every reply-worthy email already has a draft waiting in your tone.

recipe.how: Connect your mailbox, have Claude study a few dozen of your sent emails to learn your voice, then set a standing rule: classify, draft in-thread, never send.

sources.title: Caddi — Claude Code for email, what actually works
Harper Reed — Claude Code does my email

usecases.title: The Nutrition Coach That Remembers
usecases.summary: Log meals in plain language and Claude parses nutrients, tracks macros against goals calibrated to your real body data, remembers allergies and preferences across sessions, and writes grocery lists. One writer built a perimenopause-specific coach that tracked her way back to health.
usecases.example: 'Chicken liver with quinoa and red peppers for lunch' — logged, nutrient-estimated, and praised for the vitamin C + iron pairing.

recipe.how: Create a skill file with your stats, goals, and restrictions, plus a meals log Claude appends to. Log in natural language; ask for weekly reviews and a grocery list that fills your nutritional gaps.

sources.title: Aisha Yusaf — building a perimenopause nutrition coach
Claude Code Playbooks — health & fitness skills

usecases.title: The Fitness Plan That Checks Your Sleep
usecases.summary: Connect a fitness tracker via MCP or health exports and Claude builds workout plans from real data — and adjusts them: slept four hours, and it swaps the heavy-lifting day for active recovery, updating your calendar itself.
usecases.example: A custom MCP server feeding tracker data straight to Claude, so recommendations react to yesterday's sleep and strain.

recipe.how: Export health data (or build a small MCP server for your tracker), give Claude your goals and schedule, and let it plan the week — connect Google Calendar so it can move sessions when the data says to.
tools: fitness tracker data or a small MCP server

sources.title: Shanaka Chathuranga — fitness tracker + custom MCP server
Claude Code Playbooks — health & fitness skills

usecases.title: The Journaling Coach
usecases.summary: Three-minute morning prompts (intention, one focus, tiny action), evening wind-downs, and a weekly review where Claude reads all entries and names the patterns. One system analyzes each month through six perspectives in parallel and synthesizes a report.
usecases.example: A monthly report that reads thirty daily entries through six lenses — energy, relationships, work, habits — and tells you what actually changed.

recipe.how: Keep daily entries as markdown files in a journal folder. Add AM/PM prompt skills and a weekly-review command that reads the week and returns themes, one highlight, one lesson, and two small experiments.

sources.title: vystrcild — claude_code_journaling
gopet.ai — journaling with Claude

usecases.title: The Cookbook Liberator
usecases.summary: Photograph cookbook pages or drop recipe PDFs into a folder and Claude extracts everything into a searchable collection you can query by ingredient — 'what can I make with what's in the fridge?'
usecases.example: A shelf of cookbooks turned into structured markdown, searchable by ingredient, cuisine, or time-to-cook.

recipe.how: Collect photos or PDFs in a folder, ask Claude to extract each recipe into structured markdown (ingredients, steps, tags), then query the folder conversationally when planning dinner.

sources.title: Btwn Meals — 13 ways Claude makes it easier to be healthy

usecases.title: The Trip Alchemist
usecases.summary: Travel-planner skills build day-by-day itineraries with realistic timing and walking distances, backup options, visa and currency notes, and a 20-phrase pronunciation guide. A whole school of magic dedicated to trips.
usecases.example: An itinerary that knows the walk from the museum to lunch is 12 minutes, and has a rainy-day swap ready.

recipe.how: Install a travel-planner skill (or describe your dates, budget, and tastes) and let Claude web-search current recommendations into a day-by-day plan; iterate on the drafts like a picky co-traveler.

usecases.title: The Lecture-Notes Librarian
usecases.summary: Point Claude at a semester's chaos of PDFs: it reads each one, identifies the topic, renames consistently, and can produce summaries or flashcards per file — a study index for free.
usecases.example: 'week3_scan_final(2).pdf' becomes 'Microeconomics — Elasticity and Consumer Surplus.pdf', with a flashcard deck alongside.

recipe.how: Run Claude in the notes folder and ask it to read, rename by topic with a consistent scheme, and build a study index; then request flashcards or summaries per topic before exams.

sources.title: MakeUseOf — non-coding uses of Claude Code

usecases.title: The Ramble Distiller
usecases.summary: Voice-record your walking thoughts, drop the transcripts in a folder, and Claude organizes weeks of rambles into coherent themes — surfacing ideas you forgot you had and connecting ones you didn't know were related.
usecases.example: Voice memos from dog walks, clustered into three recurring themes with the original phrasing kept.

recipe.how: Use any voice-memo app with transcription, export to a folder, and ask Claude to cluster into themes, keep your phrasing, and maintain a running ideas index as new rambles arrive.

sources.title: Lenny's Newsletter — everyone should use Claude Code

usecases.title: The Photo Janitor
usecases.summary: Claude looks at each image, renames IMG_4382.jpg to what it actually shows, writes alt text, and flags duplicates — a camera roll that becomes searchable by meaning instead of timestamps.
usecases.example: 'IMG_4382.jpg' becomes '2024-08 Lisbon — tram 28 at sunset.jpg', with alt text written for every image.

recipe.how: Run Claude in a photos folder with a naming scheme; have it stage renames in a plan file first, review, then apply — and keep duplicates in a quarantine folder rather than deleting.

sources.title: MakeUseOf — non-coding uses of Claude Code

usecases.title: The Home Assistant Conjuror
usecases.summary: Point Claude Code at your Home Assistant setup and describe automations in plain English — it writes and validates the YAML (or Python API scripts), uploads them, reloads the config, and commits to git in one flow. People have furnished whole houses this way: adaptive lighting across 60+ bulbs, water-leak alerts, presence-based lighting, appliance-done notifications — and audited existing setups to surface automations that had been silently broken for months.
usecases.example: A new homeowner set up scenes, room-by-room adaptive color temperature, and humidity-triggered bathroom fans from zero, open-sourcing the whole config as idempotent Python scripts (ha-config-as-code).

recipe.how: Bridge Claude Code to Home Assistant (a HA add-on, or scripts that hit its REST/WebSocket API) and keep your config in a git repo for easy rollback. Describe the automation you want in plain English and let Claude write, validate, and reload it — start by asking it to audit your existing setup for things silently broken.
tools: a git repo for your config

sources.title: Home Assistant Community — building my smart home from scratch with Claude Code
XDA — Home Assistant was missing half its potential until Claude Code

usecases.title: The Subscription Exorcist
usecases.summary: A growing crowd is canceling monthly SaaS and rebuilding the same features as plain-text folders governed by a CLAUDE.md rules file. One writer replaced Notion and Microsoft 365 plus four read-it-later apps (Pocket, Instapaper, Readwise, Raindrop) with a queue.md / archive.md / notes.md system; another swapped Canva, Figma, and an AI scheduler for Claude skills and a calendar connector.
usecases.example: queue.md for unread links, archive.md for keepers, inline #tags instead of a database — full-text searchable, and roughly $40 a month of subscriptions gone.

recipe.how: List the paid apps you actually use and what each really does for you. For each, recreate the core as a folder of markdown with a CLAUDE.md setting the rules — a read-later queue, a notes/tasks system, meeting-note and weekly-review skills — then cancel the subscription once the plain-text version has stuck for a week.
tools: CLAUDE.md rules and a few skills

sources.title: XDA — I replaced five paid subscriptions with Claude, none were coding tools
XDA — I ditched my productivity stack for Claude Code

usecases.title: The Shared-Garden Ward
usecases.summary: Non-coders are shipping tiny household-coordination apps as installable PWAs — no App Store, no developer account. A designer who had never built an app made a shared plant-watering tracker so she and her partner stop double-watering: a garden profile, per-plant schedules, one-tap 'done', and a 'who watered last' view.
usecases.example: A plant-care PWA installed straight to the iPhone home screen via Safari, built from Figma mockups fed to Claude Code with a free Supabase backend and Vercel hosting.

recipe.how: Sketch the one screen you need in Figma (or just describe it) and hand it to Claude Code to build a Progressive Web App with a free Supabase backend and Vercel hosting. Install it to your phone's home screen straight from the browser — no Apple developer account required.

sources.title: Bootcamp (Medium) — a designer's first attempt at building with Claude Code

usecases.title: The Compounding Archive
usecases.summary: Beyond daily journaling prompts, casters are turning years of old notebooks into archives that answer back. Claude Code imports past journals into structured markdown with quote indexes and theme files, then resurfaces the right old entry when a new one echoes it — so the journal compounds instead of rotting in a drawer.
usecases.example: Wren Dougherty's open-source system: /start-day and /end-week commands file entries into predictable folders, weekly reviews build an index layer, and questions like 'how has my thinking about work changed?' get answered from the archive — with a gitignored private/ folder and commit hooks guarding the sensitive bits.

recipe.how: Start from the open-source compound-journaling setup: a git repo of markdown folders with templates, slash commands for daily and weekly rituals, and an import pass where Claude Code converts old journals into indexed, themed files. Human-readable summaries do the recall work — no vector database needed.
tools: markdown files in a git repo

sources.title: Wrench at Work — Compound Journaling with Claude Code

usecases.title: The Alphabet Locomotive
usecases.summary: Parents are conjuring bespoke learning apps for exactly one child in an afternoon. One dad built a Thomas the Tank Engine ABC app for his son — every letter a beloved character — tended 'like a stew' between breakfast and dinner while watching football, no ads, no in-app purchases, just his kid's actual obsession.
usecases.example: A is for Annie, B is for Bertie: Claude Code wrote the app from a short spec, ElevenLabs voiced the letters, DALL-E invented a 'Zhao' when no Z engine existed, and dad recorded the train whistle himself.

recipe.how: Write a one-page spec of the app your kid actually wants, then let Claude Code build it in small verified increments while you gather assets. Generate narration with a text-to-speech tool and fill any missing characters with an image generator. Ship it to the family tablet by dinnertime.
tools: an image generator for missing assets

sources.title: Rob Hunter — Thomas the Tank Engine ABCs

usecases.title: The Scholar's Familiar
usecases.summary: A /research command that spawns sub-agents to sweep your fields every morning — niche news, new papers, Hacker News — and files a synthesized digest into Obsidian. The same familiar turns dense academic papers into two-page layman's PDFs sent to a Kindle, so the reading pile actually gets read.
usecases.example: Joe Sack's daily digest checks SQL Server news, AI papers, and Hacker News before he's had coffee; he refined the skill over 300 iterations and reckons the equivalent API spend would be ~$30,000 against his $200/month plan.

recipe.how: Define a /research skill that lists your beats (topics, feeds, communities) and have it spawn a sub-agent per beat, then synthesize one digest note into your Obsidian vault. Add a second command that condenses any paper PDF into a short plain-language version for Kindle reading. Expect to refine the prompts over many mornings.
tools: optionally a Kindle for the paper summaries
